title: Checkpoint 12: Stockfish (skill 0) vs Hans
notes: Checkpoint after game 12, from the Queen's Gambit Declined: Hans plays the yardstick, Stockfish at skill 0. Nothing is studied afterwards.

moves.thought: White's Qb3 eyes b7 and adds pressure on d5, so I want to finish development safely rather than grab on c4 where the queen recaptures with tempo. Castling is solid: 6.cxd5 exd5 is a normal Queen's Gambit structure, and 6.Qxb7?? is impossible while 6.cxd5 exd5 7.Qxd5?? Nxd5 8.Nxd5 Bxg5 just loses material for White.

White's king is still on e1 with the kingside pieces undeveloped, so I want to open the position and hit the center immediately: 6...dxc4 7.Qxc4 c5! pressures d4 while White lags in development. I checked 7.Rxd8 cxb3 8.Rxf8+ Bxf8 9.axb3, which is a completely even material trade and leaves me with the bishop pair.

White's Qa4 hits my extra c4 pawn, so I want to defend it actively — note that 7...Qd5 loses the queen to Nxd5, and 7...Qxd4 drops it to Rxd4. With 7...b5 I gain a tempo on the queen; if 8.Nxb5 then a6 drives the knight back and I develop with Bb7 supporting the c4 wedge, while 8.Qxb5 Ba6 chases the queen again and keeps c4 defended with White's king still stuck on e1.

Material is actually level (my c4 pawn balances White's lost c-pawn), and White's king is stuck in the centre with the bishop and knight on the kingside undeveloped. Ba6 develops with tempo, hitting the queen on b5 while covering c4 (Qxc4 loses to Bxc4), so after the queen retreats I get a free hand with Nbd7 and c5.

White's Qa5 attacks my undefended bishop on a6, so I must address that first; Bb5 runs into 10.Nxb5 cxb5 11.Qxb5 winning a pawn, and tactics like Nd5/Ne4 fail to 10.Bxe7 Qxe7 11.Qxa6. Bb7 keeps the bishop on the strong long diagonal, and if White prepares Bxc4 with e3 I hold the extra queenside pawn with ...Qd5, where the queens face off on the fifth rank and ...exd5 would leave c4 securely protected.

I'm a pawn up and White's king is stuck in the centre with the f1-bishop and g1-knight undeveloped, so I want to develop quickly rather than grab g2 (after Bxg2 Bxg2 I just lose a bishop). Nbd7 completes development, keeps c4 protected for now (Bf1 can't reach it while e2 is blocked), and prepares c5 or Rc8 to open lines against the uncastled king.

White threatens the simple Qxc4 along the fourth rank, so I need to defend the extra pawn — and 11...Nb6 does it while simultaneously hitting the queen on a4, gaining a tempo. After the queen moves (e.g. 12.Qc2), my pawn on c4 is firmly held and I can follow with ...Nbd5 or ...h6 to untangle.

My extra pawn on c4 is only defended by the b6 knight while White eyes it with Qb5 and Bf1, so Bxc4 was a real threat; 12...Qd5 centralizes, adds a second defender to c4, and offers a queen trade, after which 13.Qxd5 exd5 gives me a rock-solid c4-d5 chain that Bxc4 can never break. I checked that Bg5 is covered by Nf3 so Qxg5 isn't on, and d5 is untouchable since White's own d4 pawn blocks the rook on d1.

I blundered my queen last move, so I must recapture on d5 in the way that saves the most — Bxd5 is best because the bishop then guards c4 (Qxc4 would lose the queen to Bxc4) and eyes f3, whereas any knight recapture or exd5 just drops the c-pawn to Qxc4 as well. I'll keep the two bishops and a solid structure and fight on.

My bishop on d5 is solid (defended by e6 and Nb6) and the c4 pawn is adequately held, so I want to gain time by kicking the queen while reinforcing d5: c6 does both, and Qxc6 is impossible since Bd5 covers c6, while Qb4/Qc5 lose the queen to my e7 bishop. I avoid Ne4/Nh5/Ng4 because they leave e7 hanging to Bg5, and I don't want h6 inviting Bxf6 since with queen-versus-pieces I'd rather keep my pieces on the board.

I'm down a queen for a knight after the earlier blunder, so I need solid, resilient play rather than tactics — Ne4 loses a piece to Bxe7, Bb4+ and Ba3 just drop to the queen, and c5 runs into dxc5 with Qxc5. Nbd7 keeps everything defended (f6 knight supported, so h6 becomes possible), unties my pieces, and if Bxc4 Bxc4 Rxc4 I can hit the rook with Nb6 for a tempo.

I'm down a queen for a knight, so I need to keep my pieces coordinated and avoid further loss — note that my Nf6 is effectively tied down because any knight move leaves Be7 hanging to Bg5. h6 gains a tempo on the bishop, unties my knight, and gives my king luft against the enemy queen; if White takes with Bxf6 I recapture with Nxf6 and keep my strong bishop pair plus the extra c4 pawn.

I'm down queen for knight after the earlier blunder, so I need activity and a bind rather than passive defence — keeping the c4 wedge pawn is key since it entombs White's f1 bishop and keeps the king in the centre. Ne4 gains a tempo by hitting the d2 bishop, is safely covered by my Bd5, and offers to trade off White's dark-squared defender; after Bb4 Bxb4 axb4 I keep the strong knight outpost and the c4 wedge.

My bishop on e7 is attacked, and since I'm the side with extra minor pieces against White's queen, I want to avoid trades that simplify toward the queen's favour — so instead of Bxb4+ I retreat with tempo-gaining activity. Bf6 keeps the bishop, puts pressure on d4, and stays defended by the g7 pawn, while Bc5 would simply drop to dxc5 and Nd2/Nc3 just lose a knight to Bxd2/bxc3.

I'm down queen-for-knight from the earlier mishap, so I need activity and structural targets rather than quiet play; Bxd4 and Nxf2 just drop material, and ...e5 dxe5 lets Bc3 reach e5 through d4. Nxc3 is forcing (bxc3 is White's only reasonable recapture, since Rxc3 Bxc3+ loses material), eliminating White's key defender of b2/d4 and the dark squares while opening the b-file for ...Rfb8/...Nb6 pressure against the weak a3/c3 pawns and the uncastled king.

I'm material down (queen for a bishop), so I need to hold my extra c4 pawn and keep pieces for counterplay; Nb6 is the only move that actually guards c4 (Qxc4?? Nxc4), since a rook on c8 is blocked by my own c6 pawn. The knight also eyes a4 and d5, and it stays safely defended by the a7 pawn against Qa5 ideas.

Since 21...c5 hits d4, and both dxc5 and d5 would open the c3–e1 diagonal for my f6 bishop (Bxc3+ winning the queen), White can't resolve the tension favourably — after 22.Qd2 cxd4 23.Nxd4 e5 I get active bishops and keep my extra c4 pawn. Alternatives like Bxd4 or Na4 just drop material (Nxd4, or b3 lines), so I play the central strike.

I'm down queen for knight, so I need maximum activity — and I noticed White's rook on b1 is completely undefended (the h1 rook's rank is blocked by Bf1). 22...Be4 hits it immediately, keeps my bishop pair and strong blockading pawns on c4/c5, and tries like 23.Qe3 or 23.dxc5 just lose the rook to Bxb1.

I'm down queen for knight, so my practical chances lie in keeping my two bishops, the cramping c4 pawn, and White's king stuck in the centre with the f1-bishop entombed. 23...Bd5 adds a second defender to c4, blocks the d-file so my rooks can later come to d8 without running into the Qd2/Rd1 battery, and keeps the dark-squared bishop eyeing c3 (so Qc3 ideas are met by Bxc3+). Lines like 24.dxc5 Nd7 or 24.dxc5 Bxf3 25.gxf3 Bxc5 leave me very much alive.

I'm down material (queen for a knight), so I want to keep my bishop pair, my c4 wedge and avoid further concessions rather than trade into a hopeless ending. My c5 pawn is currently undefended, so Rac8 protects it along the file, backs up the c4 wedge, and activates my last undeveloped piece; if White takes with dxc5 then Rxc5 gives me an active rook and a strong passer. My d5 bishop stays safe since the e6 pawn guards it.

White's Qc2 plus Bf1 are both hitting my c4 pawn, which only Bd5 defends, so I need another defender — capturing on d4 opens the c-file so Rc8 guards c4, and then Bxc4 Bxc4 Qxc4 Rxc4 would cost White the queen. It also leaves White with an isolated d-pawn that my Bf6 and rooks can harass, while my c4 wedge cramps his queenside.

I'm a pawn up with the bishop pair, and my c4 pawn is adequately defended (Bd5 and Rc8 cover it, and Qxc4/Bxc4 just loses material for White). I rejected 26...e5 because after the knight steps away my d5 bishop would be hanging to Rd1, and 26...Bxd4 gives up my bishop pair for nothing; instead Rfd8 develops with pressure on the pinned-ish knight and pre-empts the Nf5/Nxe6 tricks by adding a defender to d5.

I'm down a queen for a knight, so I must avoid simplifying trades (Bxd4 or Bxf3 only ease White's task) and instead keep my pieces coordinated around the strong c4 pawn and centralized bishop. Rc5 adds a second defender to both c4 and d5, keeps the pressure on the d4 knight, and if White tries e4 I get Bxe4 fxe4 Rxd4 winning material back. Nxe6 is only a sacrifice since f7 recaptures and my pieces cover the king.

White's a4 threatens a5, kicking my knight, so I want to stop that pawn while keeping my strong c4 wedge; 28...a5 does exactly that, and the pawn is safely defended by my rook on the fifth rank. Tactical tries fail: 29.Nb5 or 29.Nxe6 just drop a piece to Rxb5/Bxe6, and 29.b4 axb4 gives me connected passers on b4 and c4 (30.Qxc4 Rxc4 loses the queen).

I'm down a queen for a knight, so I need maximum activity and must keep my protected c4 pawn as a permanent asset. Doubling rooks on the c-file means c4 is defended three times (Rc5, Rc8, Bd5) against Qc2/Be2/Rc1, and crucially it makes ...c3 a real resource: after bxc3 Rxc3 the rook is backed up by the other rook, so Qxc3 would lose the queen.

My c4 pawn is safely defended twice (Bf1xc4 Rxc4 Qxc4 Bxc4 just loses White's queen), and Nxa4 fails to Qxa4 since the knight would be undefended. Be5 centralises the bishop, keeps the pressure on d4 and b2, and prepares ...c3, when bxc3 Bxc3+ would skewer the king and win the queen.

My bishop on e5 is hit by f4, and f6 or any other defence just loses it for a pawn, so the bishop must move; Bxd4 exd4 would trade off my active piece and hit my rook on c5, while Be4/Bf3/Bxg2 simply drop a piece to Qxe4 or gxf3/Bxg2. Bf6 keeps the bishop safe, maintains pressure on the d4 knight (so e4 can be met by Bxd4), and avoids losing a tempo to Nb5 as would happen after Bd6.

The a4 pawn is completely undefended (b2 doesn't cover it, and no piece guards it), while my c4 pawn is safely protected twice by Rc5 and Bd5, so 33.Qxc4 or 33.Bxc4 just loses heavy material after Rxc4/Bxc4. If White tries 33.b3 cxb3 34.Qxb3 I simply retreat 34...Nb6, keeping an extra pawn with a solid structure; alternatives like Be5 or g5 drop material to fxe5/fxg5, and Be4 or Bxg2 just lose a bishop.

White's immediate idea is Nxe6 fxe6 Rxd5, exploiting my bishop sitting on the d-file behind the knight, so I step the bishop off d5; then Nxe6 simply drops a piece to fxe6. Be4 is the most active retreat, hitting g2 and inviting a bishop trade, while c4 stays guarded twice by my rooks (Qxc4 Rxc4) and e8 is covered by Rc8 against Qe8+.

I'm down heavy material, so I need a real asset: advancing to c3 gives me a far-advanced pawn supported twice by my rooks, and White can't win it quickly (Qxa5 loses the queen to Rxa5, Nb5 loses to Rxb5). The one tactical try, Nxe6, fails to 35...Re5!, which defends my loose e4 bishop along the rank and traps/regains the knight (Nxg7 Kxg7 leaves White's e3 pawn hanging too).

My rook on c5 is attacked by the b4 pawn, and taking is best: after axb4 Qxb4 the rook is defended by Rc8 so the queen attack is harmless, and I get connected passed pawns on b4 and c3 backed by both rooks — my only real counterplay since I'm down heavy material. Alternatives like c2 fail to bxc5 (cxd1=Q+ Kxd1), and Rc4 or Rb5 simply drop the rook to Bxc4/Qxb5.

I'm down material, so I need maximum activity: 36...c2 attacks the rook on d1, and since the king only recaptures after promotion, the threat ...cxd1+ (new queen) genuinely wins a rook for a pawn — note 37.Qxb4?? cxd1+ 38.Kxd1 nets me the exchange. After 37.Rd2 or 37.Rc1 the pawn is held by my rook on c5, and I can follow with ...b3 to keep the queenside pawns rolling, whereas 36...Bxd4 37.exd4 just hits my c5 rook and kills my counterplay.

The rook on d1 is completely undefended — the bishop on f1 blocks the g1-rook along the first rank and can't cover d1 diagonally — so my c2 pawn simply promotes with capture. After cxd1=Q I win a whole rook, my new queen attacks both Bf1 and Nd4, and White's tries (Qe8+ or Nxe6) fail to Qxf1+ or fxe6.

My bishop on e4 can drop into c2, where it is defended twice by my rooks and attacks the queen on d1 — Nxc2 Rxc2+ then Qxc2 Rxc2+ leaves me a clean bishop up, and Qxc2 Rxc2+ Nxc2 Rxc2+ leaves equal pieces with my extra passed b-pawn. Any queen retreat other than d2 just loses it, and the counter-shot Nxe6 fails to Bxd1.

My bishop on c2 is attacked twice (Qd2 and Nd4) but defended twice by the doubled rooks on the c-file, so Nxc2 Rxc2 Qxc2 Rxc2+ actually wins material for me; the real loose point is the b4 passer. Rc4 defends b4, attacks the knight on d4, keeps c2 doubly guarded, and after Qd3 I even get Be4 hitting the queen (Qxe4 Rxe4).

White's bishop just took my rook on c4, so I must recapture with 40...Rxc4, even though my c2-bishop is then hit twice (Nd4 and Qd2) and defended only once — after 41.Nxc2 I keep rook, dark bishop and the passed b-pawn, which gives more counterplay than 40...Bxd4 41.Qxd4 where my loose light bishop also falls prey to Qd3/Bxe6 tricks.

My bishop on c2 is attacked twice (Qd2 and Nd4) and only defended once, so I must eliminate the knight — and 41...Bxd4 does it, since 42.Qxc2 Rxc2+ 43.exd4 would hand me the queen for a bishop, so 42.exd4 is forced. After that I keep rook plus the active light-squared bishop, and 42...b3 gives my passed pawn a solid bishop escort while White's d4 pawn becomes loose.

White's Rc1 piles on my c2-bishop (Rc1 + Qd2 vs only Rc4), so Rxc2 Rxc2 Qxc2 would simply win a piece; moving the bishop lets Rc1 take the undefended rook on c4. The move ...b3 solves everything: the pawn gives c2 a second defender (after Rxc2 bxc2 my pawn is one square from queening with the rook behind it), and it also takes away d3/b1/d1 squares since my light bishop already covers them.

I'm down a lot of material, but my rook on c4, bishop on c2 and pawn b3 form a mutually-defending bind — if White tries Rxc2 Rxc2 Qxc2 then bxc2 and my pawn promotes, so his breakthrough needs the king on d3 first. Tactical tries like Rxd4 (Qxd4) or Bd3 (Rxc4 bxc4) just shed material, and b2 loses to Rxc2, so I'll keep the structure intact and make a safe waiting move with my king while keeping e6/f7 solid.

White's Rf1 was played to cover b1, but pushing 44...b2 solves that: my bishop on c2 guards b1, so Rb1 would just lose the rook to Bxb1 (after Qxb1 I'd have R+B+pawns against a lone queen). That means White's queen gets permanently tied to guarding the promotion square, which gives me by far the best practical chances in a bad material situation.

White's Qe2 threatens both Qxc4 (on the d3-diagonal) and Qxc2, so I must cash in my passed pawn immediately — material only balances if the new queen eliminates White's rook. After 46.Rxb1 Bxb1 I have rook+bishop versus queen with my rook hitting d4 and f4, and if instead 46.Qxc4 then 46...Bd3! forks the queen and the rook on f1 while being defended by my new queen.

White's rook on b1 just captured my new queen and is now completely undefended, while my queen on e2 — his queen on e2 cannot reach b1, so the rook is simply free. Taking it leaves me rook plus bishop plus four pawns against queen plus four pawns, and it's the only way to keep material; any other move (like Rxd4) just loses my loose bishop on c2 to Rxc2.

I'm down a queen for a bishop, so my only goal is to keep the bishop safe and hold my pawns together; Bc2 and Ba2 drop to Qxc2/Qxa2, Bd3 loses to Qxd3, Bf5 loses to gxf5, and Be4 invites Qxe6 hitting the bishop on the e-file. Bg6 keeps the bishop on a safe square where it still guards f7 and can meet a future f5 push.

White's Qc7 hits f7, so I need to cover it — Kg8 defends the pawn with the king and keeps my structure intact for now. Alternatives like Be4 or Bf5 just drop f7 immediately, and f5 gxf5 exf5 strips my pawn shelter, so I'll hold with the king.

I'm down a queen for a bishop, so my only practical hope is to build a fortress around the king and pawns; e5 or f5 just loosens things (e5 dxe5 leaves my e-pawn gone and f7 exposed). Kh7 keeps the king active, adds a second defender to my bishop on g6, and maintains the f7/g7/h6 pawn shield against Qd8+ or Qd7 ideas.

I'm down a queen for a bishop, so my only hope is to make the position as hard to crack as possible; f6 would unguard e6 (Qxe6 hitting my bishop) and f5/h5 just loosen my pawn shell. Kg8 keeps g7 guarded twice-over by the king, keeps the e6-f7-g7-h6 chain intact and avoids any immediate tactic.

I'm lost material-wise (queen vs bishop), so my best practical hope is to trade off pawns and head for a position where White has fewer breakthrough options; 51...h5 forces matters on the kingside before White gets g5 in with tempo. After 52.gxh5 Bxh5 my bishop stays active and I keep the e6/f7/g7 shelter, and Qb8+ Kh7 doesn't win g7 since my king guards it.

I'm down a queen for a bishop, so my only hope is to trade off as many pawns as possible and aim for a position where my bishop can blockade. Capturing hxg4 eliminates one of White's four pawns and forces the king to recapture, after which Bh7 keeps the bishop safe behind the h-pawn.

My g4 pawn is hanging to the king, and both Bf5 and Bh5 would drop the bishop to the queen along the fifth rank (b5-h5 is clear). Advancing f5 guards g4 with a pawn, and the f5 pawn itself is backed by e6, so it can't simply be taken.

White's Qd7 hits both e6 and g7, so I need a move that covers them; Bf7 defends e6 and blocks the queen's path along the 7th rank, keeping g7 safe (Qxg7+ would just lose the queen to Kxg7). Bh7 or Kh8 would drop e6 immediately, and e5 just loses a pawn to dxe5, so Bf7 is the most solid.
Only two legal moves: Be8 drops the bishop immediately to Qxe8+ since e8 is undefended by my king on g8. Kh7 sidesteps the check and keeps the bishop, even if White can keep probing with Qd7.

I'm hopelessly material-down (queen for bishop), so the e6 pawn can't be saved by anything; my priority is keeping the pawn chain intact. Bg6 defends f5 and keeps my structure glued together, and if White grabs with Qxg6+ Kxg6 I reach a pawn ending where my g4/f5 wedge gives real drawing chances since d4-d5 would just leave me a pawn up.

White's queen on e7 hits the undefended e6 pawn, and both Bf7 and Be8 simply drop the bishop to the queen on e7; Bh5 leaves the bishop loose to Qe8 ideas. Kh8 would let Qxe6 attack my bishop on g6 with no defender, so Kg8 is best: after Qxe6+ Kh7 my bishop is guarded by the king and I stay as solid as possible.
I'm in check from Qe6, and my bishop on g6 is attacked and undefended, so Kf8 and Kh8 both drop it, while Bf7 loses the bishop to Qxf7+. Kh7 answers the check and defends the bishop at the same time.

My bishop must stay on g6 to guard f5 (any bishop move drops f5 with check and likely more), so this is a king move; Kh6 walks into checks like Qh8+ with my king getting loose and g4/g7 falling. Between Kg8 and Kh8, both allow Qf6/Qe6+ hitting my undefended bishop, but I can always answer by returning to h7 where the king covers both g6 and g7, and Kg8 keeps me off the h-file and the a1-h8 diagonal.

I'm hopelessly down material, so I just want the most solid shuffle: Kh7 keeps the bishop on g6 guarding f5 while my king still covers g7, and Qxg6+ is impossible since the queen would be captured. Bf7 would attack the queen but abandon f5, and Kf8 walks into checks from d8/e7 squares.

I'm material-down but my bishop on g6 holds f5 and my king shuttles between g8 and h7; Kh6 would allow Qf6 hitting both g7 and my bishop, and bishop moves abandon f5. Kg8 repeats the position after 59...Kg8, so I keep heading for a threefold repetition draw.

Be8 just drops the bishop since nothing defends e8 (Qxe8+), and Kf7 puts my king on open diagonals inviting checks like Qb3+ that could pick off my pawns. Kh7 keeps the king safe next to the g7 pawn, keeps the bishop guarded by the f5/g4 structure, and repeats the position for drawing chances.

Both Be8 (Qxe8) and Bf7 (Qb7 hitting the undefended bishop on the seventh) simply drop my last piece, and Kh6 allows Qh8+ forcing my king out to g5 into a mating net. Bh5 is the only move that keeps the bishop safe (nothing attacks h5) while still covering the e8 square along the e8–h5 diagonal.

White's Qf8 threatens Qxf5+, since f7 and f6 are empty, so I must cover f5; Bf7 and Be8 just drop the bishop or the pawn, and Kh6/Kg6 allow Qxf5 or Qf7+ with more harassment. Bg6 is defended by my king, shields f5 (which in turn holds g4), and keeps g7 covered by the king so Qxg7+ is impossible.

I'm lost material-wise, so my only practical hope is to blockade the d-pawn and pick it off: Bf7 immediately hits d5 and keeps the e6/d7 blockade squares available. White can harass with Qc7 or Qf8, but the bishop simply steps to e6 where it attacks d5 and covers d7, whereas Bh5 or king moves let the pawn run d6-d7-d8 unopposed.

My bishop is light-squared, so it can never capture the d-pawn, but it can control the d7 square — Be6 blocks the pawn's advance immediately. White will hunt the bishop with Qc8, but I can retreat along the a4-e8 diagonal (Bb3-a4) to keep guarding d7 and prolong resistance.

My bishop on e6 is hanging to Qe5 and it's the only piece holding back the d-pawn, so I must relocate it while still covering d7. Bc8 keeps d7 under control, stays off the queen's current lines, and is harder to harass than Bd7 (which drops to Qa4).

My g7 pawn is attacked and I can't defend it with the light-squared bishop, so I keep the bishop on the key d7 square with Be6, blocking the passed pawn's path. If White grabs with Qxg7+ Kxg7, I get bishop plus two pawns against three pawns, with the d-pawn permanently blockaded by my bishop — real drawing chances.

White's d-pawn is the real threat, so I want to stop it physically: Bd7 blocks the pawn and is not attacked by the queen on a8 (which only covers the 8th rank, the a-file and the a8-h1 diagonal). Other bishop retreats like Bc8 drop the piece to Qxc8, and quiet moves allow d7 followed by promotion, so Bd7 gives me the most resistance.

My bishop must stay on the c8–d7–e6 diagonal, since from there it simultaneously controls d7 (stopping the pawn's promotion) and defends f5, which in turn keeps my g4 pawn protected from Kxg4. Be6 keeps both of those duties while leaving the king on h7, where the rank check from a7 is blocked by my g7 pawn and the b1–h7 diagonal is blocked by f5; if White hits the bishop with Qe3 or Qa2 I simply retreat to d7 or c8 and hold the same net.

My bishop on e6 is the only thing holding back the d-pawn (if d7 then Bxd7, since the queen on a8 doesn't cover d7), and Bd5 would simply drop the bishop to Qxd5 while Bc8 drops it to Qxc8, so I shouldn't move it. Instead I make a safe king move, keeping the bishop's grip on d7; on h6 I'm not exposed to any discovered check and my g7 pawn stays defended.

I'm lost material-wise (queen vs bishop), but my bishop on e6 is the only thing holding back the d-pawn, since d7 would be met by Bxd7; so I must keep it there and shuffle my king. Kh7 is the safest king move, avoiding Qe8+ ideas that come after Kg6 or Kh5, and g5 just gives White another passed pawn with check.

My bishop on e6 is the only thing stopping d7 and promotion, so I must not move it — and I can't retreat to d7 since Qa7 would then pick it off on the seventh rank. That leaves a king waiting move, and Kg8 keeps the king near the corner with g7 defended and no immediate checks of consequence.

Bc8 loses immediately to Qxc8+, so that's out. Kf7 exposes my king to a barrage of checks along the 7th rank and the f-file, whereas on h7 my king is tucked away and my bishop on e6 keeps covering d7 and c8 to stop the pawn. I'll keep the solid setup with Kh7.

Bd5 and Bc8 and Bg8 all hang the bishop to the queen on the long diagonal or the 8th rank, Bf7/Bc4 let d7-d8 queen, and Kh6 runs into Qh8#, since g5 and g6 are covered by the f4- and h5-pawns. So I'll play g6 to eliminate the dangerous h-pawn and give my king the g7/g6 escape squares.

The queen on b7 already covers d7, so Bd7 and Bf7 both just drop the bishop immediately (Qxd7 / Qxf7+), and even after a king move White wins the bishop with d7. Between king moves, Kh8 allows hxg6 with the mating idea Qh7# (pawn-supported), and Kh6 walks into Qg7+ with my king stripped bare, so Kg8 keeps the most escape squares (f7/f8/h8) and avoids immediate mating nets.

I'm in check on the 8th rank, and Bc8 just loses the bishop to Qxc8+, so I must move the king; I want to keep the bishop on e6 guarding d7 to hold the passed pawn back. Kf7 brings my king toward the d6 pawn and avoids lines like Kg7 hxg6 Kxg6 Qg8+ where a queen check on the g-file also forks my bishop.

Bd7 just drops the bishop to Qxd7+, and Kf6 exposes my king in the open, so I'll step back to g8 where I'm safest. Returning to g8 also repeats the position after 76.Qb7+ Kg8, so I'm steering toward a threefold repetition in this lost material situation.

I spotted that White's immediate threat is Qg7#, since the h6 pawn defends g7 and the queen covers f7/f8/h7/h8 — and with the king on g8 or h8 that's mate; my light-squared bishop can never guard g7, and blocking on the 7th rank (Bd7/Bf7) just loses the bishop with check. Only Kf8 keeps an escape route via e8/e7 after Qg7+, so despite h7 coming I have to play it.

Bc8 blocks the check but the queen simply takes it along the open eighth rank (Qxc8+), losing my only piece. Kf7 steps out of check and keeps the bishop guarding the d7 promotion square, so it's the only sensible try.

I must keep the bishop on e6 since it alone stops d7 and queening, so Bd7 (losing it to Qxd7+) is out. Among the king moves, Kg8 runs into h7+ driving me off, and Kf6 exposes the king to further checks, so Kf8 is the most solid interposition-free retreat while the bishop holds d7.

Qb8+ is a check along the eighth rank; Bc8 blocks but simply loses the bishop to Qxc8+ with the d-pawn still queening, whereas Kf7 steps out of the check and keeps my bishop guarding the d7 square and the promotion path. It's lost long-term, but I'll keep the pieces and make White work for it.

I'm in check and must respond; Bd7 simply loses the bishop to Qxd7+, and Kf6 lets White push h7 and promote since my king is too far from the corner. Kg8 covers both h7 and h8, blunting the h-pawn for now while the bishop still guards d7 against the d-pawn's advance.
